title: Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
description: Comedian and actor Russell Brand reflect
body:
Comedian and actor Russell Brand reflected in a car window as he left Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.
                
                    Alberto Pezzali/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alberto Pezzali/AP
    

   
   London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.   Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.   "I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."   Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.   
   Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.   He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.   Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.   Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."   "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."   The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.   Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.   
   In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.   Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.   He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan he met backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.   The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.   Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.   The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.   Brand said in the witness box that the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.   "My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.   Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.   Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.   His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

title: What's next for Democrats after the midterms. And, a look at the outstanding races
description: Democrats' First 100 Hours, Outstanding Midterm Races, Trump Doubles Down On Policies
body:
Democrats' First 100 Hours, Outstanding Midterm Races, Trump Doubles Down On Policies
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-152046/nx-s1-mx-6030264-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Democrats won this week in districts and states that President Trump carried by double digits just two years ago. The party now has its largest Senate majority since the passing of the Affordable Care Act during Obama's early presidency. Senate results from Alaska and Mississippi are still pending. If those races favor Democrats, their majority could grow to 54, plus the two independents who caucus with them.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The sun rises behind the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday.
                
                    Allison Robbert/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Allison Robbert/AP
    

   
   🎧 A few tight House races remain uncalled, but the swing toward Democrats already rivals the post-Nixon Watergate backlash, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. She highlights two notable race surprises that happened this week. One was in Nevada's 2nd District, which has been Republican since the 1980s. Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson claimed victory overnight. The other was in Alabama's 2nd District, where Shomari Figures overcame redistricting that favored Trump by 14 points. Figures won by more than seven points.➡️ Mike Johnson plans to step down as top House Republican in the new Congress after a tough defeat for his party, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.➡️ Voters in 39 states, Washington, D.C., and the Northern Mariana Islands decided on 146 ballot measures covering issues like taxes, transgender rights, traffic cameras and data centers. Here's a summary of the results.   
   For more than a year, Democrats urged voters to elect them to lower costs and eliminate corruption. Now, the party must act to fulfill its campaign promise. The new Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law, but Democrats plan to launch ambitious investigations in the House and Senate. Democratic Party leaders and political analysts shared their insights with Morning Edition on the midterm election results, discussed the impacts of mid-decade redistricting efforts and outlined the party's next steps.   🎧 Most legislation still requires 60 votes to pass the Senate, and Trump has fluctuated between saying he will be Mr. Veto and expressing willingness to work with Democrats, NPR's Sam Gringlas says. Democrats are interested in restoring enhanced ACA health subsidies, reversing Medicaid cuts, asserting control over tariffs and pushing to end the war with Iran. Gringlas says this election has intensified pressure on Democrats. He points to a voter he met this summer, who said that if Democrats gained control, they would have to enact real changes, otherwise it wouldn't matter who they nominated for president in 2028.   Trump focused on his East Wing ballroom construction project during his first public appearance after the Republicans lost the House and Senate. When asked about the election, he said he wasn't to blame for his party's losses.   
   🎧 Trump quickly pointed out that he wasn't actually on the ballot, NPR's Emily Feng says. But he did urge voters to imagine he was. Voters associated his signature policies, like tariffs and the war in Iran, with rising inflation and gas prices. After Vice President JD Vance posted on social media yesterday suggesting that the war in Iran contributed to GOP losses, Trump somewhat agreed. The president cited its impact on pump prices, but doubled down on the war, saying he would act the same way again if he had to. With a Democratic Congress, Trump will encounter greater legislative gridlock, and Democrats could wield stricter funding controls on issues like immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict in Iran, Feng says.➡️ A new Democratic majority could pressure Trump to end the war in Iran. But directly influencing fuel prices, which are tied to the complex international oil market, will be challenging.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Jan Hakan Dahlstrom/Getty Images/Stone RF
    

   
   Have you ever found yourself drowning in a sea of your own mail or other documents? Well, it is time to tackle that paper chaos. Don't panic. Kacy Paide, a professional organizer with more than 20 years of experience, has shared tips with Life Kit to make the task less overwhelming.   ✉️ Focus on your closest pile and separate it into active and inactive ones. Active items require follow-up, like calls or bill payments, while inactive items do not.✉️ Clearly mark the due date on active documents with a bold, permanent marker on a sticky note.✉️ Save important documents like birth certificates, passports, product manuals, tax papers and medical records. Choose a method that suits your habits: alphabetize, color-code or simply label. For easy access, place vital documents in a brightly colored folder.✉️ You don't need to shred everything that has your name and address on it. The Federal Trade Commission advises destroying documents containing sensitive information, such as account numbers, birth dates, passwords, signatures and Social Security numbers, to protect against identity theft.✉️ Start small by dedicating just 25 minutes to decluttering. Remember, organizing is an ongoing process that needs regular maintenance and adjustments.   
   Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The destroyed location of the original Cafe 11/11 in Kherson, Ukraine.  CREDIT: Svet Jacqueline for NPR UKRAINE
                
                    Svet Jacqueline for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Svet Jacqueline for NPR
    

   
   In Ukraine's Kherson region, a brief ceasefire brought a momentary return to normalcy. Brokered by first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo last week, the truce allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate from a Russian-occupied town and provided a rare few days of peace in a frontline city. Russia and Ukraine agreed to the deal to help Oleshky, a town near Kherson that was occupied by Russian troops in 2022. The troops had mined the land around it, and food and medicine were rarely able to reach the people. This short pause in hostilities was a welcome relief, allowing families to fill the sidewalks, shoppers to hurry to stock up and cafe-goers to enjoy art-filled spaces. These photos capture a brief glimpse of everyday life for these people.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Election cake is a sweet civic tradition dating back to 1771. The annual Election Cake Bake-Off at Connecticut's Old State House in Harford, CT, has continued the celebration for more than 250 years.
                
                    Barbara Glassman Dell
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Barbara Glassman Dell
    

   
   At Connecticut's Old State House, the annual Election Cake Bake-Off has been celebrating the sweet civic tradition of election cake for more than 250 years. This dessert has evolved from what it once was: a tough fruitcake, often soaked in alcohol.Chemical manufacturer 3M has reached a $7.35 billion settlement to resolve thousands of personal injury claims related to toxic chemicals found in firefighting foam. (via PRE News & Ideas)A new study shows that loon populations are declining across the birds' southern breeding range, but Maine stands out with a slight increase in loon productivity, according to Birds Canada. (via Maine Public)   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election
body:
Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks during an election night watch party on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Bottoms will be the nation's first Black woman governor.
                
                    Megan Varner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Megan Varner/Getty Images
    

   
   Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app      Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the future path to power for Democrats and Republicans alike must run through the South.   Black voter turnout surged in states like Louisiana and Georgia, as Democrats flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Mississippi is too close to call.   Republican-led efforts to redraw House districts to gain more favorable districts in places like Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and Florida backfired, with Democrats poised to net several seats in the region.   
    Loading... 
   In several states, the margins at the top of the ticket were so large that the blue tsunami carried down-ballot races along with it, flipping several state legislative chambers and statewide offices along the way.   Even in contests where Democrats ultimately did not prevail, the millions of dollars of investment from both sides and the wide-ranging repudiation of the Trump administration from every demographic group highlight the South's important role in control of Congress and the White House in future election cycles.   Redistricting   In the aftermath of a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act, Republican-led Southern states rushed to redraw House maps to create additional seats that would better withstand a midterm environment where voters punished the party in power.   They included changes in Tennessee that split Memphis into three districts (and where Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson is within a few thousand votes of winning), a redraw of several Alabama districts that sought to unseat Rep. Shomari Figures (who won by nearly 8 points in the new Trump +14 configuration) and a target of nine seats in Texas and Florida.    Loading... 
   As of Wednesday night, Republicans have won one of them, according to a race call by the Associated Press.   Before Election Day, there were signs that the ruling, along with the war in Iran, rising costs, concerns about corruption with the Trump administration and other top issues would serve as a motivator for turnout among Black voters.    
   In primaries held after the ruling, Black voter participation soared. Ashley Kennedy Shelton with the Louisiana-based Power Coalition for Equity and Justice previously told NPR that the court decision was "personal" for Black voters.   "Everybody's spending more money on their electricity bills, their gas bills, their food bills," she said. "All of these different things are really personally impacting voters. And I think that for all the folks that used to say, 'I don't do politics!' I think they realize that politics is absolutely doing them, and they have to get involved."   In South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a U.S. Senate seat, the state saw record voting for a gubernatorial election year, driven in part by elevated Black turnout. It's a similar story in Louisiana, where Democrat Jamie Davis narrowly lost to Sen.-elect Julia Letlow by less than 2% in a state President Trump won by more than 15 points in 2024.   
   Mississippi's Senate race is too close to call, with Democrat Scott Colom leading by less than 1,200 votes against incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state with the highest share of Black voters in the country.   
   State level   It's not just Congress where the South is the center of shifting power. Big Democratic victories — or swings away from Republicans — at the top of the ticket led to an avalanche of shifting offices at the state and local level.   Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's 18-point victory in Georgia helped propel former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to victory in the governor's race, as Democrats swept every single statewide elected office, gained control of the state utility regulator, and are set to win a majority in the state House.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this file photo from the 2026 election, people wait to vote in early voting for the midterm elections on Oct. 25 in Cary, N.C.
                
                    Allison Joyce/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Allison Joyce/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper's 20-point victory was enough to potentially flip multiple congressional seats and win control of the state House.    Texas Democrats won a majority of seats in their state House, while Republican House supermajorities in Florida and South Carolina have ended, too. The down-ballot gains extend into states that aren't as purple or blue, with dozens more pickups reported in Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky and Tennessee.   2028 is now   The expansive majorities in the House and Senate built upon southern swings have implications far beyond the makeup of the next Congress, as both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election.     
   In the leadup to Election Day this year, potential presidential contenders from both parties have made varying efforts to offer financial support and campaign for nominees in tight races, including notable appearances by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, chair of the Democratic Governors Association.   On the Republican side, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Vice President JD Vance are among those who focused on the region.   Even though Republicans held on to the Florida governor seat and U.S. Senate seat, closer-than-expected margins in statewide races and House races alike make the state an attractive investment for both parties seeking to gain an edge with voters for 2028, just like Democrats' romp in historically red Texas.   
   Together, Texas, Florida, Georgia and North Carolina represent more than a third of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the White House.

title: Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
description: Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rig
body:
Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, accompanied by her aides, speaks during a news conference at the Justice Department in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 29, 2025. Dhillon resigned on Thursday.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
    

   
   The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.   Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.    Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.    "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."   
   In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."    "We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.   
   During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.   The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.   Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.   "We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."   
   Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.   In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.   Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.   The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.   
   In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.    "I'm proud of all we've accomplished during this time to ensure our nation's civil rights laws protect every American," she wrote in the email, a copy of which was obtained by NPR. "I'm also grateful for the hard work of the dedicated employees within the Division and the rest of the Department of Justice."   For many division veterans who were highly critical of Dhillon's treatment of career staff and her enforcement goals, her departure was a welcome development.    "Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."   "Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

title: Democrats will take control of Congress next year. What does it mean for the economy?
description: The Democratic gains in this week's midterm elections will bring a different business climate to Washington. But the overall economy should be
body:
The Democratic gains in this week's midterm elections will bring a different business climate to Washington. But the overall economy should be OK.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    LEILA FADEL, HOST:  Economic anxiety was a big driver of this week's election results. Now that most of the votes have been counted, is anything about the economy likely to change? NPR's Scott Horsley joins us now to talk about this. Good morning, Scott.SCOTT HORSLEY, BYLINE: Good morning, Leila.FADEL: So Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate next year. What does that mean for people's pocketbooks?HORSLEY: In the short run, it may not mean a whole lot. We know that voters are very unhappy about the high cost of living, and Democrats capitalized on that frustration to win big majorities in both the House and Senate. But Joe Brusuelas, who's chief economist at the accounting firm RSM, says Congress does not necessarily have the power to bring those high costs under control.JOE BRUSUELAS: The two quickest ways to improve affordability would be to remove the tariffs that we put on our major trading partners in Canada and Mexico and find a way to wrap up hostilities in the Middle East, which over time would provide relief via the gas pump. Until those things occur, I'm not holding my breath.HORSLEY: A Democratic Congress could certainly try to reassert control over trade policy and the war, but the president does have the veto pen. And it's not clear the new majority's going to be able to overcome that. Democrats say they will try to find some bipartisan common ground.FADEL: Now, the stock market rallied once the election results were clear. What does that say about what's in store for the economy?HORSLEY: Yeah. The Dow soared more than 1,500 points yesterday. I think part of that is just relief that the election results were decisive and we're not going to have weeks of limbo or legal challenges keeping everyone in suspense. Dan North, who's a senior economist at the insurance company Allianz Trade, says markets tend to like it when the two parties have to share control of Congress and the White House.DAN NORTH: This is divided government. And usually this is when the economy does best because it allows Washington to do what it does best, which is nothing.FADEL: (Laughter).HORSLEY: It's a little exaggeration to say the government's going to do nothing for the next two...FADEL: Right.HORSLEY: ...Years. But divided government does tend to rein in the excesses of both parties. And, you know, to the extent there's gridlock, at least that's predictable, and business knows how to deal with that.FADEL: Are there particular industries that stand to gain or lose as a result of this week's election?HORSLEY: One of the big losers is Elon Musk, who spent $400 million in what turned out to be an unsuccessful effort to support Republican candidates. Two companies Musk leads - Tesla and SpaceX - are both headquartered in Texas, which will soon have a Democratic governor and U.S. senator for the first time in decades. Stock in both those companies fell yesterday even as the wider market was soaring.Defense contractors, private prisons - they may not do as well with a new Democratic Congress. On the other hand, clean energy and healthcare companies could get a boost if Democrats are able to restore some of the federal funding that the GOP Congress had cut. Now, the elections also brought more restrictions on data centers and artificial intelligence. And Brusuelas says that could be a good thing for all the other industries that have had to compete for the resources with the AI juggernaut.BRUSUELAS: This will result in a better-balanced economy, a better-balanced composition of growth.HORSLEY: Even AI leaders have said they would welcome some government oversight. One other thing to watch for is whether there's any kind of renewed push to address immigration, especially after the big swings in Latino voters. You know, the number of available workers has actually shrunk on President Trump's watch, partly because of the aggressive crackdown on both legal and illegal immigration. Unless the U.S. finds a way to allow more legal immigration, it's going to end up with a smaller workforce, and that means a smaller economy.FADEL: That's NPR's Scott Horsley. Thank you, Scott.HORSLEY: Good to be with you, Leila.

title: After sweeping midterm wins, here's what Democrats hope to get done in the majority
description: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D
body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks as House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., look on during a press conference at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   For more than a year, Democrats hammered one message at every opportunity: put Democrats in charge, and Congress will take action to lower costs and stamp out corruption.   Democrats will soon have that chance when they take control of the House and the Senate after a rout of Republicans at the ballot box.   Now Democrats have to unite a sometimes fractious caucus around a game plan for fulfilling that central campaign promise.   The first 100 hours   Democrats say that in the first hundred hours, they want to restore enhanced Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts Republicans passed last year in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that are about to take effect.   
   They also want to reassert Congress' authority over tariffs and try to force an end to the Iran war by bringing new votes on war powers resolutions. These are priorities on which Democrats have near-total agreement.   Despite controlling both chambers with substantial margins, Democrats will still be operating in the confines of divided government.   Most legislation still needs 60 votes to avoid a filibuster to pass the Senate, and President Trump has vacillated between promising to be "Mr. Veto," and saying he is open to working with Democrats.   
   "I want us to get to the work of passing legislation," Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senator-Elect from Michigan, said in an interview last week. "If Trump vetoes that, it's on him. But I think you're going to see a whole lot of Republicans thinking twice about whether they want these Medicaid cuts for example to go through."   Congress has other tools, like withholding funding for the war through the appropriations process, must-pass legislation that will require some compromise across the aisle despite Democrats now being in the driver's seat, says Molly Reynolds, an expert on Congress at the Brookings Institution.   "But when you have a wave election like this, the seats in the other party that get taken out often tend to be the more moderate end of that party," she says. "And so that leaves you with a large Democratic majority, but also a comparatively more conservative Republican conference."   
   Investigations will also be a major focus for Democrats now emboldened by subpoena power.   The top Democrat on the House Oversight committee, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., released a two-word statement on election night directed at Trump and his orbit: "Lawyer up."   Bold, dramatic change   The next likely House Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., told reporters on Wednesday that Democrats will usher in "bold, dramatic change."   What exactly that looks like is a work in progress.   This fall, House Democrats organized working groups to figure out how to address the costs of gas and groceries, utilities, housing and caregiving. Each is helmed by two Democrats, one from the progressive wing of the party, the other more to the center.   "We'll have a family conversation when we get back, and certainly in the new Congress, about what's the best way to do that beyond what we know we need to do immediately," Jeffries told reporters when asked about different approaches to addressing health care costs.   
   Some newly-elected Democrats ran on a pledge to press for Medicare for All. Others ran promising more gradual steps to expand access to health insurance and cut costs.   Hints of the coming debate appeared even before the election.   Number three Senate Democrat Brian Schatz of Hawaii, told CNN, "If we want to be more aspirational, if we want to make more bold policy changes … that's for 2028. Right now it's about stabilizing the country itself."   "Nobody thinks this election was about going back to the status quo or being the party of nervous lawyers that tinkers around the edges," Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told reporters on Wednesday.   All the same message?   Top Democrats this week are downplaying that tension.   "If you listened to our candidates, whether they were progressive or more moderate, they were saying the same things," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters. "You talk about it in Maine differently than you talk about it in Kansas, but it was all the same message."   
   In the House and the Senate, a large chunk of the new majorities will be made up of more moderate Democrats who flipped conservative-leaning districts and traditionally red states, like Iowa, Kansas and South Carolina. A new class of progressives is also preparing to join Congress, some who also flipped Republican-held seats.   Will Lawrence, just elected to Congress from a Republican-held battleground district in Michigan, says in addition to tackling costs and corruption, voters across the political spectrum want to see action not only to end the war in Iran, but also to halt tax dollars going to Israel.   
   "People are desperate and hungry for change," Lawrence told reporters on Wednesday. "They don't want to see this happening on our dime and with our weaponry."   The ability of progressives to move the agenda to the left will be more limited than they may have initially anticipated because the Democratic majorities will not be narrow.   "We had the right candidates in the right districts at the right time," Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., who chairs the campaign arm of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, told reporters on Wednesday. "[Jeffries] has the flexibility to lead. No more discussion of leveraging the speaker."   But the bright lines between progressives and moderates are also less defined than in the past, as a new crop of Democratic candidates weld together facets of economic populism with more moderate positions on other issues like immigration, energy and social issues.   There are Democrats across the spectrum, for example, who want Congress to move on reigning in artificial intelligence and data centers.   
   Such a sweeping wave election for Democrats will also amp up the pressure to act, giving voters high expectations about what the party will be able to accomplish quickly.   "We shouldn't overpromise at the risk of underdelivering," Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider, who chairs the New Democrats caucus, said in an interview.   As Joel Rutherford, a local Democratic activist in Macomb County, Michigan told NPR in an interview over the summer, "If the Democrats, hopefully, take the Senate and take the House, they better do something, OK? People better see some real change."   
   Rutherford said if they don't, it won't matter who Democrats nominate for president in 2028 because getting them elected will be a tough sell.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand on the Democratic Party's agenda for the next Congress

                Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., attends a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in Washington on April 30, 2026.
                
                    Graeme Sloan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Graeme Sloan/Getty Images
    

   
   Democrats have won back Congress. Now comes the harder question: How much can they actually change with President Trump still in the White House?   "I dare him to veto that," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York told Morning Edition, challenging Trump to reject bipartisan legislation restoring Medicaid coverage.   
   Gillibrand said Democrats would focus on lowering costs, restoring health care access and ending the war in Iran.   Democrats also face pressure to hold the Trump administration accountable, with new investigative powers and the possibility of a third impeachment.   Asked about impeachment, Gillibrand did not commit to pursuing it.   "We can do both," she said, proposing a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and senior administration officials.   
   Like other Democrats, Gillibrand cited the war in Iran as a factor in the party's election victories, saying Trump had broken his promise to avoid prolonged wars as the conflict drove up costs.   "We have to end this war in Iran," she said.   Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the war had contributed to Republicans' election losses. But the conflict continues, with Iranian officials warning against renewed U.S. attacks. How Democrats intend to bring the war to an end remains unclear.   In her interview with NPR's A Martínez, Gillibrand also discussed Democrats' gains in Republican states, Trump's ballroom and cuts to food assistance and medical research.   Listen to the full conversation by clicking the blue button above.    The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

title: Democrats will control Congress. Will it change Trump's approach to foreign policy?
description: NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with historian and journalist Anne Applebaum about how much a Democrat-led Congress can steer foreign policy.
body:
NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with historian and journalist Anne Applebaum about how much a Democrat-led Congress can steer foreign policy.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    LEILA FADEL, HOST:  For more on how the midterm results and a new Congress may affect U.S. foreign policy, we're joined by Anne Applebaum. She's a historian, staff writer at The Atlantic and host of the podcast "Autocracy Of America (ph)." Good morning, and welcome back to the program.ANNE APPLEBAUM: Oh, thanks for having me.FADEL: So how will this election, seen as a stunning rejection of the president and his policies, change the way the world views the United States?APPLEBAUM: The most important shift in perception of the United States has come from the fact that the U.S. no longer, under Trump, saw itself as the leader of the democratic world, as a member of a big alliance in Europe and Asia and as a country who opposed autocracy and dictatorship elsewhere. This election, first of all, will restore especially our allies' confidence in our democratic system, that it hasn't been undermined and destroyed, and will give some people a hope that eventually we'll return to the leadership role that we once had.FADEL: Now, one of the countries that is not an ally was really gleeful over this, and that's Iran. State-linked accounts were mocking the U.S. president saying, oh, he wanted regime change in Iran, and he got it in the U.S. Do you expect to see the administration's approach to Iran - the war that Americans clearly don't approve of - to change?APPLEBAUM: I don't expect Trump to change because Trump doesn't - you know, he doesn't think in terms of political influence. He's not that interested in what Americans think of his policies. But I do think that once the new Congress is seated, you will see pressure to end the war coming from them. You could see them trying to use the power of the purse, the appropriations committees to end the war or to influence politics. And so I think that will change the trajectory of the war sooner or later.FADEL: What else can they do from Congress? I mean, you talked about the power of the purse. So basically, we won't fund this?APPLEBAUM: So you will see investigations. Some of these will be corruption investigations into the - and remember that this is a president - the first president actually that we've ever had who uses the tools of American policy to enrich people around himself. And so you'll see investigations into that. But you may also see investigations into, for example, the behavior of the secretary of Defense, Pete Hegseth, questions about his competence, questions about the kinds of advice that the president was receiving.And, you know, because Congress can't force the president to make changes. The president does have the ability to veto legislation, but establishing a different narrative, both about this war and more broadly about American foreign policy, is something that Congress can do if it moves fast out of the gate, if its leadership thinks hard about what its priorities are and if it chooses the right messaging.FADEL: Now, there has been bipartisan support for Ukraine in Congress, and yet Ukraine isn't getting what it says it needs. And Europe has been panicking that Russia's war ambitions will expand. Do you expect anything to change?APPLEBAUM: I do expect a - the bipartisan coalition that supports Iran and that, by the way - excuse me - that supports Ukraine, and that, by the way, reflects the views of the country. The Americans also support Ukraine. I do expect them to become more active. I would expect legislation forcing the president to reimpose sanctions. I can't tell you right now whether that's veto-proof, but it's not impossible that it could be because the support is so strong.I expect, again, committee's investigations into the question of why Starlink was cut off unexpectedly. You know, the shenanigans that have taken place around the negotiation process, the fact that the negotiators were simultaneously trying to do business deals while negotiating with Putin and with Zelenskyy. I expect all of that to become more open, more part of the conversation, more part of criticism. And as I said, I would expect sanctions legislation.FADEL: Now, the war in Iran, many Americans blame for the pain they have when it comes to affordability, affording gas. But tariffs also has had an impact, and that's an area of international policy where Congress historically plays a role. What do you expect to happen there?APPLEBAUM: No. I expect Congress to use its ability to block the president, you know, by saying, we won't appropriate money. I expect them to use that actively.FADEL: Anne Applebaum is a historian and staff writer at The Atlantic. Thank you so much for your time and your insights.APPLEBAUM: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF DR. DRE, MARY J. BLIGE AND RELL SONG, "THE MESSAGE")

title: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
body:
The government submitted final renderings to the National Capital Planning Commission that depict a 250-foot arch topped with three gold statues and an eternal flame.
                
                    Department of the Interior
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Department of the Interior
    

   
   Thursday could be a make-or-break day for President Trump's triumphal arch.   For months, the Trump administration has barreled toward his dream of building a 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C.: rubber-stamping and side-stepping various federal reviews, cutting out Congress and announcing imminent construction despite a lack of final approval and an ongoing legal battle.   In May, the entirely Trump-appointed Commission for Fine Arts approved the arch's design — still incomplete at the time. In September, a federal council packed with Trump allies abruptly terminated a historic preservation review that participants had already criticized as rushed.   
   It all comes to a head on Thursday, when the National Capital Planning Commission will meet to consider final approval for the controversial structure. The arch is the only item on the agenda; the meeting will be online-only and is expected to take five hours because of the high volume of public participation.   More than 130 concerned citizens have signed up to speak, an unusually high number for such meetings and a symbol of the widespread public opposition. Democratic lawmakers, veterans, historic preservationists and more than 100,000 people have spoken out against the arch in written comments, local protests and previous commission meetings.   Among their many concerns, critics say the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital.   The White House has repeatedly said the arch will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery" and be "one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world."   
   "It will be one of the great things we've ever done," Trump said from the Reflecting Pool on Monday, giving the arch — alongside several other D.C. construction projects — valuable airtime in his last in-person remarks before the midterm elections.   The planning commission is widely expected to greenlight the arch. It approved preliminary site and building plans over the summer, and its new Trump-appointed chair, Mark Paoletta, expressed his enthusiastic support for the arch in an op-ed published last month. The administration says that after a successful commission vote, all that's needed to break ground is sign-off from its own Department of the Interior.   
   In fact, the government notified a federal judge late last month that, pending those two approvals, "construction could commence as early as" Thursday.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Trump wants to build his arch on the grassy traffic circle on Arlington Memorial Bridge, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery (the entrance to which is seen in the background). The house on the top of the hill formerly belonged to Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee.
                
                    Saul Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   It filed that notice as part of the ongoing lawsuit brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian who argue the arch is unlawful without approval from Congress. The Trump administration has not sought that, instead citing Congress' century-old authorization of a pair of columns on that traffic circle that were ultimately never built.   The plaintiffs promptly asked District Judge Tanya Chutkan to issue a preliminary injunction before Thursday's meeting to block the administration from "taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction, of any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization" while the case plays out.   
   A group of advocacy, historic preservation and conservation organizations quickly signed on to a supporting brief. At a hearing last Friday, Chutkan heard from both sides and expressed skepticism about the government's sense of urgency and national security claims. Then, over the weekend, D.C. and Virginia jointly filed their own lawsuit, calling the arch "flagrantly illegal" for a whole host of reasons.   Chutkan has consolidated the two cases, with all eyes on her docket as Thursday's meeting ticks closer.   On Monday, the judge ordered the government to notify the court within one hour of any arch decision by the National Capital Planning Commission, National Park Service and Department of the Interior — and to provide notice within 30 minutes of "any activity related to or in preparation for the construction of an arch on Memorial Circle."   Chutkan's order suggests she may wait to issue a ruling on construction until after the planning commission meeting, which is scheduled to adjourn at 6 p.m. ET.   On Tuesday, the Trump administration asked Chutkan to clarify and to modify her order to require 24 hours' notice instead, explaining that even though its staff is "working diligently (including nights and weekends) on this matter, it takes time for decisions to be communicated through the various chains and then appropriately drafted into a notice suitable for filing with the Court."   
   The plaintiffs responded with their own filings, opposing that request. They compared the situation to that at D.C.'s East Potomac Park, where the government provided the judge in that case less than a full day's notice before cutting down 430 trees during a holiday weekend.   "Indeed, Defendants recently demonstrated how much they can change the status quo in a matter of 24 hours," the lawyers wrote.   The judge later clarified her wording but kept the timeline the same.   Hours later, on Wednesday night, the government notified the court that Grunley Construction Company, a Maryland-based firm, "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval."   On Thursday morning, dozens of protesters gathered at Memorial Circle for a rally that turned into a hearing watch party. The protesters, some wearing veteran hats, sang "We Shall Not Be Moved" accompanied by a small accordion.    The rally, organized by Third Act — an advocacy group for older Americans — featured a 21-foot bamboo-and-vinyl arch replica. The height of the group's faux arch was bound by National Park Service rules, said Lisa Finn, one of the organizers.   "They're very strict on that, which is kind of funny because they're thinking about putting this honkin' arch that's going to be 250 feet high," Finn said.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Paint marked potential digging locations on the grass of Memorial Circle, as seen on Thursday morning. The Trump administration later told the court it believes a construction company painted the lines on Saturday.
                
                    Ava Berger/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ava Berger/NPR
    

   
   People on site quickly noticed that painted white lines marked the grass beneath their feet, apparently marking potential digging locations. Photos of the paint took off online — prompting the Trump administration to file another notice with the court. The government said it found out Thursday midday that the construction company had painted those lines on Saturday, "as best as can be determined at this juncture," without proper authorization.    Along with veterans and organizers, Rep. Don Beyer and Rep. James Walkinshaw, both Democrats from Virginia, spoke at the rally.   
   "If somehow Donald Trump manages to build this arch," Walkinshaw said. "I'm not going to stop until we ensure it's a temporary arch. The proposed location, just steps from the country's largest military cemetery, "is an area where we celebrate service and sacrifice to our nation. Two things that Donald Trump knows not a damn thing about," he said.   As the hearing began, organizers set up in two separate tents — one to livestream the proceedings and another to give their testimony, via live video.    Paoletta said he expects the hearing to last into the evening. The livestream stopped working just over an hour into the meeting, shortly after public testimony began.   How we got here — and what could happen next   One of the many people signed up to speak was Michael Lemmon, the veteran and retired foreign service officer for whom the lawsuit is named. Lemmon has said he hopes to be buried in Arlington National Cemetery one day — but not if there's an arch.   "The thought of being interred in the shadow of what I believe to be a personal vanity project is profoundly disturbing to me," he wrote in a court filing in February, when the case was first filed.   
   The arch would stand 250 feet tall in Memorial Circle, a traffic circle on the bridge that links D.C.'s National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. It would be more than twice the height of the nearby Lincoln Memorial and, by the National Park Service's own admission, disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby monuments.   Renderings submitted to the planning commission show a white concrete structure topped with three golden statues, including a winged woman holding a torch with an eternal flame.   That flame was one of the recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which said in September that the arch would not pose a hazard to airspace as long as it is continuously lit a certain way. Aviation safety experts told NPR that those unconventional lighting recommendations add a new layer of risk — like glare and fire hazards — to an already troubling proposal.   
   Just days after the FAA released its report, Trump announced on social media that the arch would actually serve as a military complex housing snipers and ammunition. Legal experts saw that abrupt rebrand as an attempt to cast the arch as a matter of national security, an argument that has so far helped the administration proceed with its controversial White House ballroom.    The final renderings sent to the planning commission don't mention drones or snipers. But in a seven-page declaration submitted to the court last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the arch a "generational national defense opportunity."   On Friday, Chutkan questioned how the government would square installing military equipment with accommodating what it has said could be up to 22,000 civilian visitors per day.   "The arch is somehow supposed to deter assassination attempts on the president?" she said, in response to the government attorney's answers. "It's going to be completed three years from now."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Mark Paoletta, the Trump-appointed chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, pictured at its meeting in October. The commission is tasked with evaluating and approving federal construction projects in D.C.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   As the legal battle over the arch intensifies, one of the Trump administration's primary arguments is that the veterans don't have standing to sue. They point to the Supreme Court's ruling in the ballroom case, though Public Citizen — the group representing the veterans — says the two are very different.   It's in that context that the Democrat-led governments of D.C. and Virginia jumped into the fray with their own lawsuit this weekend. Their 55-page complaint details their grounds for suing as well as the "battery of irreplaceable injuries" they say their communities will suffer "as soon as construction begins — from disruptions of local traffic to environmental degradation to threats to security and emergency preparedness."   The jurisdictions argue that the arch is illegal without congressional authorization and violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws as well as D.C.'s restrictions on building heights.   
   They say an arch would "substantially disrupt daily life in the capital region," including by forcing local governments to divert resources away from other priorities. The lawsuit says an arch at that location would increase traffic and hinder emergency response along one of the main corridors between D.C. and Virginia, complicate the flight path of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and threaten local wildlife, all things that governments would have to spend time and resources addressing.   They also have concerns about the construction process itself — from 320-foot cranes disrupting already-complex airspace to excavation work sending sediment into the Potomac River.   
   "These harms cannot be remedied if construction of the Arch proceeds," the complaint reads, adding that "the unlawful construction of a project of this scale will be difficult to undo."   
   The Trump administration has said construction will take two to three years, with crews working 20 hours a day, year-round. It said in a court filing last week that the first six months will involve underground excavation and foundation work, arguing that there is no need for a judge to intervene at this stage because plaintiffs' concerns about the lost view would not be relevant.   But lawyers for D.C. and Virginia say the administration "would suffer no cognizable injury if required to wait before beginning construction of an illegal monument."   "Defendants cannot plausibly claim they have an urgent need to begin building the Arch 101 years after enactment of the statute that they (wrongly) claim authorized its construction and over one year after the President announced his intention to build it," they wrote.   Critics have accused Trump of trying to rush approval of the arch before this week's midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers filed a supporting brief in the suit. Several have vowed they will not let the arch proceed if their party retakes control of Congress, and doubled down on those claims after Tuesday's Democratic sweep.    "My bill to stop it has 80 co-sponsors now. It'll have more than 200 by the time we reconvene in January," Beyer, who won a seventh term this week, said at Thursday's rally. "In the meantime, we're trusting the U.S. courts to do their job and to stand up to this."

schema.headline: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
